Issued at 245 AM CDT Fri Aug 21 2026

A shortwave trough is pivoting across the northern Great Lakes 
early this morning and has been leading to the development of 
some isolated to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms in 
WI, southeastern MN, and eastern IA. This festering of showers 
is expected to continue through daybreak with a few of these 
showers possibly making it into portions of far northern and 
northwest IL. However, with the dry air mass across northern IL 
and northwest IN and cloud bases with these showers generally 
around 10000 ft any rain should struggle to reach the ground 
locally aside from perhaps a stray sprinkle. Therefore, expect 
dry conditions to prevail through the rest of the night with 
just some passing clouds from time to time. Though, some shallow
ground fog may continue to develop in north-central IL and 
northwest IN where temperature-dew point depressions are low 
(around 1-2 degrees) and result in some locally reduced 
visibilities around 3-5 miles through daybreak. 

The aforementioned shortwave will continue to pivot eastward 
across northern MI this morning which will allow the trailing 
shortwave in northeast ND to pivot into the Upper Midwest and 
then eventually northern IL later today. Ahead of this secondary
wave is a cold front that will also be drifting towards our 
area. As these features approach, winds will become more south-
southwesterly and begin to advect in the more humid (higher dew 
point) air in MO into northern IL and northwest IN. Couple this 
warm-moist advection with daytime heating and cooling mid-levels
with the approaching shortwave, conditions are expected to 
become unstable and favorable for showers and thunderstorms by 
midday. Therefore, expect scattered showers and thunderstorms to
begin to take shape around 12-1 PM CDT in northwest IL and 
gradually drift south and east across the rest of the area 
through mid to late evening. 

In addition to the favorable thermodynamics, a jet streak on 
the southern periphery of the shortwave looks to generate around
30-35 kts of effective shear overhead which should allow for 
some storms to become better organized and become capable of 
severe weather. While damaging winds (up to 60-65 mph) and hail 
(up to half dollar size) look to be the main threats, stout 
westerly 850-700 mb flow will allow for some low-level turning 
and may result in a threat for an isolated tornado or two. With 
the better overlap of the low-level shear and surface 
instability forecast to be across north and northwestern IL 
(namely areas west of the Fox Valley and north of I-80), the 
Storm Prediction Center has upgraded this part of our area to a 
slight risk (level 2 of 5) for severe weather today. Though, all
of our area will have the potential to see some severe weather 
today and thus remains under at least a marginal (level 1 of 5) 
risk. Furthermore, locally heavy downpours will also be possible
with the showers and storms today but with their progress 
nature and lower PWATs the threat for flooding is low at this 
time. 

Heading into tonight, the shortwave and cold front should push 
through northern IL and northwest IN around midnight and should 
bring an end to the shower and thunderstorm activity. Though, a 
few lingering showers (15-20% chance) cannot be ruled out in 
northwest IN tonight. Otherwise, expect dry conditions tonight 
with overnight lows dipping into the low to mid-60s. 

While mostly dry conditions should prevail through the day on 
Saturday, broad upper troughing is forecast to still be over the
Great Lakes region with a couple of embedded disturbances 
expected to be pivoting through northern IL and northwest IN 
which may result in a few showers or storms Saturday afternoon. 
Forecast soundings on Saturday do show that the mid-levels 
should be drying out as the aforementioned disturbances pivot 
overhead which should limit the coverage of any showers or 
storms, but have opted to maintain a slight chance (15-20%) 
mention in the forecast just in case any isolated activity is 
able to materialize. The bigger weather concern on Saturday 
however, will be the increasing northwest winds (gusting around 
20-30 mph) which will result in building waves and an increasing
threat for rip currents at area beaches. Initially, the highest
waves will be in Porter County, IN on Saturday but with the 
breezy winds expected to linger into Sunday that the larger 
waves and dangerous currents will spread into the rest of 
northwest IN and northeast IL by Saturday night. A Beach Hazard 
Statement will likely be needed for this time period so make 
sure to keep to check the forecast before heading to the beach 
this weekend and remember to stay dry when waves are high!
